lessons.title: Supply, Demand, and the Anatomy of Boom and Bust

children.text: The Three Forces Behind Every Boom and Bust

The previous lesson laid out the four-phase shape of a commodity cycle: oversupply, stabilisation, demand catching supply, and boom. That is the what. This lesson is about the why. Three structural forces, working together, explain almost every commodity boom and bust you will ever study: supply takes years to respond, demand barely reacts to price in the short run, and inventories amplify whatever imbalance is left over. Understand these three, and the crude oil, gold and metals cycles in the chapters ahead will stop looking like unpredictable chaos and start looking like a mechanism.

body.text: Booms happen because supply cannot react quickly. Busts happen because supply eventually overreacts. The lag itself is the cycle.

children.text: You cannot build a copper mine in six months. Discovery, permitting, financing and construction for a new mine commonly takes a decade or more from the day a viable deposit is confirmed. Offshore oil fields are similar: five to ten years is a normal gap between discovery and first oil. This lag means that when demand suddenly rises, the industry cannot simply switch on more supply. Prices have to rise far enough, and stay high for long enough, to justify locking up capital for a decade against the risk that prices fall before the project is even finished.

US shale oil broke this pattern partially, and that break is why oil cycles have become shorter and choppier since the mid-2010s. A shale well can go from a drilling decision to first oil in a matter of months, not years. This is why the 2014 to 2016 oil crash bottomed out faster than earlier oil busts, and why shale producers are often called the industry's swing suppliers.

children.text: Force 2: Demand Barely Moves With Price, in the Short Run

markDefs.definition: How much the quantity demanded changes in response to a change in price. Inelastic demand means quantity barely changes even when price moves a lot.

children.text: A factory that needs steel for a contracted order does not stop buying steel because the price rose ten percent this month. A commuter does not stop driving to work because petrol got costlier by a few rupees a litre. In economist's language, short-run demand for most commodities is highly

. That inelasticity is precisely why small mismatches between supply and demand produce large price moves: there is no quick, cheap way for either side of the market to adjust, so price has to do all the work.

Over the long run this changes. Higher fuel prices eventually push buyers toward more fuel-efficient vehicles or electric ones. Higher steel prices eventually push builders toward alternative materials. But long run in commodity markets often means several years, which is exactly the kind of lag that lets a short-term imbalance turn into a full-blown price spike before the demand side of the equation starts to respond.

columns.label: Short Run (months)
points: Demand is largely fixed by existing habits, contracts and infrastructure
A price spike mostly gets absorbed, not avoided
This is where the sharpest price moves happen

columns.label: Long Run (years)
points: Buyers can switch technology, suppliers or materials
High prices themselves encourage the substitution that eventually kills the boom
This is how every historical commodity boom has eventually ended

children.text: Force 3: Inventory Turns a Small Gap Into a Big Price Move

Unlike a stock, most physical commodities need somewhere to sit while they wait to be used: a tank, a warehouse, a storage yard. That storage has a finite capacity, and when it fills up, the market has nowhere left to absorb a surplus except through price. This is exactly what produced one of the strangest events in market history.

body.label: WTI Crude Oil Turned Negative
body.context: On 20 April 2020, the expiring May WTI futures contract settled below zero. Storage tanks at Cushing, Oklahoma were running out of space during the Covid demand collapse, and traders holding contracts they could not take physical delivery of ended up paying buyers to take the oil off their hands.

body.text: Gold almost never behaves this way, because gold is cheap to store relative to its value and virtually none of it is consumed. That is one of the first hints of why gold's cycle, covered in Chapter 3, runs on a completely different logic from oil and industrial metals.

body.title: Stylised Cycle: Price vs New Supply Coming Online (Illustrative, Not Actual Data)

children.text: Read this chart as a story, not as data. Demand rises in Year 1, but because supply cannot respond quickly (Force 1) and existing demand will not shrink to meet the shortfall (Force 2), price runs far ahead of any real change in production. High prices eventually justify the investment decisions that supply needed all along, but those decisions take years to turn into actual output. By the time that new supply arrives, in Years 4 and 5 here, demand has often cooled and the market is oversupplied again, sending price down just as fresh capacity keeps arriving. That mismatch between when price turns and when supply turns is the entire mechanism behind the four phases from the previous lesson.

body.title: Apply the Framework
body.scenario: MCX copper falls 15% over a single month on reports of weaker Chinese construction activity. No mine has closed, no mine has opened, and actual global copper consumption over the month has fallen by less than 2%.
body.prompt: Using the three forces from this lesson, explain why a 2% change in real demand could plausibly produce a 15% price move.
body.modelAnswer: The price move overshoots the fundamental change because of how inelastic and inventory-driven commodity markets are in the short run. Traders and consumers cannot verify the true state of Chinese demand in real time, so a weak data point gets read as a signal about future demand, not just current demand, and gets priced in immediately even though actual usage has barely moved. Because copper supply cannot adjust quickly (Force 1), producers cannot signal 'we'll just produce less to match demand' in a way that stabilises price. And because a small oversupply has to sit in inventory somewhere (Force 3), even a modest surplus can push visible stockpiles up sharply in percentage terms, which further spooks price. None of this means the 15% move is 'right' or 'wrong', only that in a market built this way, sentiment about future demand can move price far more than the current change in actual tonnes bought and sold.

points: Supply lags demand by design: mines and oilfields take years to build, so supply cannot react quickly to a demand surprise.
Demand is inelastic in the short run: buyers mostly keep buying through a price spike, which is exactly why the price has to move so much to balance the market.
Storage and inventory amplify small imbalances into large price swings, and when storage runs out entirely, as it did for WTI crude in April 2020, prices can behave in ways that seem to defy logic.
These three forces together, not any single cause, are what turn an ordinary supply or demand shift into the boom-and-bust pattern you will see repeatedly in oil, gold and metals.
